title: Germany's states · GeoClick Geography
edition: Regions of Europe · one lesson per country · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Germany's states, part 1 of 1. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
We work through 16 of the Germany regions the map names, once each: where it sits, one fact worth keeping, and a hook to remember it by.

states.name: Schleswig-Holstein
lines: Schleswig-Holstein fills the far north of Germany between Denmark and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, on both the Baltic and the North Sea, with Kiel on the canal.
Denmark ruled it until Prussia took it in 1864, and the border was only settled by a plebiscite in 1920, which is why Danish schools survive in the north.
Remember the very top of Germany, crossed by the Kiel Canal, the busiest artificial waterway in the world, with more ships than Suez and Panama together.

states.name: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
lines: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern runs along the Baltic coast in the north-east, east of Schleswig-Holstein, with Rostock as its largest city.
It is the emptiest state in Germany, with fewer people to the square kilometre than any other, and it is full of lakes.
Remember the empty Land with its painted chalk cliffs, and with Rügen and Usedom, Germany’s two largest islands, off the coast.

states.name: Hamburg
lines: Hamburg is a small city-state on the Elbe in the north of Germany, far smaller than the Länder around it, with Schleswig-Holstein above it and Niedersachsen below.
Its name comes from Hammaburg, a ninth-century castle, and it is officially the Free and Hanseatic City, which still shows in its number plates, HH.
Remember the small port city-state with more bridges than Venice, Amsterdam and London put together.

states.name: Bremen
lines: Bremen is a tiny city-state in the north-west, far smaller than Niedersachsen all around it, and it is really two towns, Bremen and Bremerhaven, with the mainland in between.
Its name comes from bremo, Old Saxon for the edge, because the town stood on the bank of the Weser where the ground rose above the marsh.
Remember the smallest Land, two separate towns with Lower Saxony in the gap, and the statue of the town musicians who never actually got there.

states.name: Niedersachsen
lines: Niedersachsen spreads across the whole north and north-west of Germany, from the Dutch border to the Elbe, with the Wadden Sea along the coast and Hanover in the middle.
Lower means downriver, towards the sea, not southern, and the Saxons who gave Sachsen its name started here before the name travelled south-east with a duke’s title.
Remember the biggest Land after Bayern and the flattest, where the tide empties the Wadden Sea twice a day.

states.name: Berlin
lines: Berlin is a small city-state in the north-east of Germany, completely ringed by Brandenburg and touching no other Land.
It is really an island inside Brandenburg, and the two voted on merging in 1996 and said no.
Remember the enclosed city-state that voted to stay on its own, with more museums than rainy days in the year.

states.name: Brandenburg
lines: Brandenburg wraps all the way around Berlin in the north-east and reaches east to the Oder, with Potsdam as its largest city.
It is the cradle of Prussia, where the Margrave of Brandenburg became the King in Prussia and everything from there to Königsberg followed.
Remember the state that circles Berlin, with three thousand lakes that make it the weekend of the whole capital.

states.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
lines: Sachsen-Anhalt lies in the centre of Germany between Brandenburg and Thüringen, with Magdeburg on the Elbe.
The state was only invented in 1945, joining Prussian Saxony to the old principality of Anhalt, a name that sounds like the German for hold on.
Remember the post-war state, with Luther nailing his theses in Wittenberg and Bach born just over the border in Eisenach.

states.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
lines: Nordrhein-Westfalen fills the whole west of Germany, from the Netherlands and Belgium down to the southern Rhineland, with Essen as its largest city and the Ruhr around it.
It is by far the most populous state, with one German in five living here and a quarter of them in the Ruhr, whose coal and steel built modern Germany.
Remember the crowded western Land of the Ruhr, where the last pit closed in 2018 after two centuries of mining.

states.name: Thüringen
lines: Thüringen is the wooded state in the centre of Germany, between Hessen to the west and Sachsen to the east, with Erfurt as its largest city.
It is called the green heart of Germany, and it is the geographic centre of the country as well as the wooded one.
Remember the green heart, where Weimar was the home of Goethe and Schiller and the birthplace of the Bauhaus.

states.name: Sachsen
lines: Sachsen is the large state in the east of Germany, reaching the Polish and Czech borders, with Dresden as its largest city.
The Saxons never actually lived here; the name arrived in 1423 with the margraves of Meissen, six hundred kilometres away from where the Saxons really were.
Remember the Land where the first true porcelain outside China was fired at Meissen in 1708.

states.name: Hessen
lines: Hessen sits in the centre of Germany and touches six other Länder, including Rheinland-Pfalz to the west and Bayern to the south, with Frankfurt as its largest city.
Its name comes from the Chatti, a tribe Tacitus wrote about, and Chatti became Hessi and then Hessen.
Remember the middle state whose landgraves rented soldiers to Britain in the 1770s, so American schoolchildren learn the word Hessians.

states.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
lines: Rheinland-Pfalz lies along the Rhine and the Moselle in the far west of Germany, with Koblenz as its largest city and Saarland tucked into its south-west.
The Pfalz is Latin palatium, a palace, because the Count Palatine was the emperor’s deputy and his lands kept the title.
Remember the wine state, which grows two thirds of German wine, and Mainz, where Gutenberg printed the first book with movable type around 1450.

states.name: Saarland
lines: Saarland is the small state in the far south-west of Germany, bounded by Rheinland-Pfalz on the north and east and by France and Luxembourg on the west and south, with Saarbrücken as its largest city.
It voted twice on its own future, in 1935 to rejoin Germany and in 1955 against independence, so it joined West Germany in 1957 as the very last piece.
Remember the last piece to arrive, the smallest Land apart from the city-states, where the Saar loops back on itself at Mettlach.

states.name: Bayern
lines: Bayern is the biggest state by area, filling the south of Germany from the Alps up past Munich, which is its largest city.
It is the oldest state here, a duchy from 555 and a kingdom from 1806, and it joined the German Empire in 1871 while keeping its own army and postal service.
Remember the great southern Land, which holds half of all German ground above a thousand metres, and Neuschwanstein, the model for Disney’s castle.

states.name: Baden-Württemberg
lines: Baden-Württemberg is the south-western state, running from the Black Forest in the west across the Swabian Jura, with Stuttgart as its largest city.
The two names were welded together in 1952, and Baden is Old High German for baths, after the Roman springs at Baden-Baden.
Remember the merged Land of 1952, where the Danube rises in the Black Forest and Mercedes and Porsche are both built around Stuttgart.

recap: 16 regions of Germany, one for each target of the map: Schleswig-Holstein, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Hamburg, Bremen, Niedersachsen, Berlin, Brandenburg, Sachsen-Anhalt, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Thüringen, Sachsen, Hessen, Rheinland-Pfalz, Saarland, Bayern and Baden-Württemberg.
Remember the shape of Germany from the inside: the regions nest around each other, and every name on the map belongs somewhere in this one country.
